messages.subject: [statnet_help] STERGM and bipartite networks
messages.body_plain:
Dear Statneters,

is there a limit how many sime slices a bipartite network in a STERGM model can have?

When I create 10 random networks of the same size:

g <- list()
for (i in 1:10) {
g[[i]] <- network(5, bipartite=10, density=0.2)
}

and construct a model which only acconts for the first two networks

model1 <- stergm(g,
                  formation = ~ edges + b1star(2) + b2star(2),
                  dissolution = ~ edges + b1star(2) + b2star(2),
                  estimate = "CMLE",
                  times = 1:2)

everything runs fine.
But if I include more than 2 networks, e.g.

model2 <- stergm(g,
                  formation = ~ edges + b1star(2) + b2star(2),
                  dissolution = ~ edges + b1star(2) + b2star(2),
                  estimate = "CMLE",
                  times = 1:4)

I get the following error:

Error in combine.networks(y0s, standardized = TRUE, blockname = ".stergm.CMLE.time.index") :
  Bipartite networks are not supported at this time.

any ideas?

Best
Sebastian


--

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have been studying the Butts (2008) paper on Relational Event Models. 
The approach is definitely powerful. What I seem to miss is how it 
differs from a Cox proportional hazard model. If we consider a Cox model 
with time-varying covariates and assume every edge to be at risk always 
and events are allowed to recur everytime, wouldn't we end up with the 
same model? I have the feeling something must be different between these 
models, but what is it exactly?

Eric Quintane has a few papers where the REM is estimated as a Cox 
model, but he uses an ordered set of events in his papers, rather than 
time-stamped events.

So, my question: when modeling a time-stamped event sequence, how does 
the model differ from a Cox model?

Thank you,
Peter Verbeet

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Visualizing a Changing Social Network
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

My name is Kate Chandler and I am a masters student at the University of British Columbia.  I would like to visualize a social network that changes over time, so that it looks something like this<http://www.archivalscience.ca/communities.gif> (you might need Chrome to view it, and the visualization starts after a couple of seconds.)

I am using a subset of the Enron Email Dataset, which includes only the top ten emailers.  You can see this dataset here<http://www.archivalscience.ca/enron_bigplayers.csv>.

My previous attempts to visualize this data has been confusing to the viewer, because the layout switches the position of the vertices from one time frame to another.  My previous attempts to visualize the network are visible here <http://www.archivalscience.ca/igraph.gif> (igraph static images of time-based subsets of the dataset shown one after the other) and here <http://www.archivalscience.ca/bigplayers_movie.gif> (ndtv animation).

To make clear the changing social network, I plan to create custom software.  So far, this is my general strategy:

First, run the igraph's fastgreedy algorithm on time-based subsets of the dataset, and for each subset run the igraph function "community(fg)" which creates a list of groups of vertices.  Then, get the program to randomly select a vertex within a group and assign it a set of coordinates.  The other vertices in this group would be given an offset of this original coordinate so that the entire group is positioned together on the graph.  This would be repeated for all groups of vertices.

In the next increment of the dataset, the program would again begin with the same first selected vertex of each group, and would again put vertices of the same group close to one another together.  Vertices which have left their original group to form new groups, should be shown as moving from their parent group toward their new group.

So I am trying to figure out several things: how to assign a coordinate to a vertex, how to assign an off-set coordinate to vertices in the same group, and how to animate the movement of vertices away from their parent group.

Any ideas or suggestions would be much appreciated.

Kate Chandler

Candidate, MAS/MLIS
School of Library, Archival, and Information Studies
University of British Columbia
Email: kate.chandler@ubc.ca<mailto:kate.chandler@ubc.ca>

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm's that adjust for network size and composition effects
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] ergm's that adjust for network size and composition effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi Statnet community,

I have been working with some agent-based modelers, and I received a question from them that I didn't know the answer to. Can one of you please help out? The question pertains to Pavel and colleagues' 2011 paper, Adjusting for network size and composition effect, and is quoted below.


One of the points that the Krivitsky et al. - 2011 paper made was how the network statistics are derived from an egocentric census. E.g., network level properties calculated via f(x_i,x_j) are slightly modified when considering egos and alters (equation 4), whereas actor level statistics are unchanged (equation 5). So this got me thinking about the types of statistics that can be extracted from not just a single level egocentric sample, but what if you ask the alters who THEY talked to etc. (i.e., snowball or forest fire sampling) and if there were any assumptions that Krivitsky's paper makes that would need  to be adjusted to include those. Specifically, in their discussion section they state:
"We limit our statistics to first- and second-order effects - dyadic and degree distribution effects - and do not discuss third-order effects such as triad-closure bias, and while two of the notions of locality that we describe allow modeling of such effects, we do not examine the properties of these in the presence of an offset, because the egocentrically sampled data available do not contain information about such effects."
This is what prompted my question about any follow up work that they've done in this area, as they hinted at wanted to do something in the future (at that time, and maybe in the past now!).

Thanks,
Aditya Khanna
University of Chicago

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Specifying missing/unobserved edges in a network object
messages.body_plain:
HI Pavel,

Thanks for your response. I paraphrase the problem in a hypothetical scenario below.

Consider 30 participants recruited for a public health study. We have information on their online Facebook network, say they are connected to a  total of 130 individuals. Thus, we have information on all ties for the first 30 individuals, but for the next 100, we only know of their tie(s) to the 30 participants. We have no information on the ties that might exist between these 100 individuals. 

I am interested in identifying sets of most "central" nodes (via different algorithms, eg. betweenness, bridging, key player, etc). But our assessment of such centralities will be incorrect because we don't have information on all edges in the network. Therefore, one possible approach is to use ergm's to model the unobserved edges, between the 100 Facebook friends of the study participants, to get a complete picture of the network, before applying graph centrality algorithms. 

I thought one way to mark edges as being unobserved is in the `network` package, by setting the value of an edge equal to NA, as opposed to 0 or 1. For a network object `net`, if I wanted to mark an edge between nodes i and j as NA, I could do the following:

net.edges[i,j, add.edges=TRUE] <- NA

If I iterate the above process between all nodes that have unobserved ties, the goal is accomplished, in theory at least. In practice, given the size of Facebook networks, the above process is simply too slow. I didn't see a need here to write a custom MH proposal, but maybe I am missing something?

Thanks,
Aditya

messages.subject: [statnet_help] recent statnet package releases: ndtv and tsna
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] recent statnet package releases: ndtv and tsna
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

Just a quick update to say that the statnet team has released the alpha 
version of the 'tsna' (Temporal Social Network Analysis) pack to CRAN.
The new package has:

* Code for finding forward temporal paths through networks which will 
hopefully serve as the basis of lots of extensions of centrality measures.
* Tools for evaluating durations of ties, rates of change, etc
* Measures of sequence (Gibson?s p-shifts) from the relevent package
* Static projections of dynamic networks
* And of course it has wrappers for evaluating standard ?static? SNA 
metrics at multiple time points and returning a time series (using the 
ergm and sna packages).

A vignette for tsna is located here:
http://cran.fhcrc.org/web/packages/tsna/vignettes/tsna_vignette.html

please let me know if you have questions or see issues :-)


Yesterday we also released an update to the 'ndtv' package for 
visualizing temporal networks. It has some neat new features, including 
the ability to easily embed animations as widgets in Rmarkdown 
documents. I wrote a blog post with a quick overview here: 
http://skyeome.net/wordpress/?p=775

And a heads up, we've been previwing a new ergm release and hope to have 
it up to CRAN very soon.  In addition to bug fixes and features, this 
will get rid of the warnings like:

"Warning: replacing previous import by ?network::as.edgelist.network? 
when loading ?tergm?"

which you may have been seeing due to the migration of some functions 
from ergm to network in the last network release.

best,
  -skye

messages.subject: [statnet_help] STERGM and bipartite networks
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Richard,
> Specific to my case: I'm still trying to figure out how to implement
> an ergm for a bipartite network with continuous node covariates
> similar to the b1factor ergm term - something like b1nodecov or some
> such.
That looks like an omission that we probably should remedy in the next
release. For the moment, the following workaround should work. Let b1x
be a vector of actors' covariates, b2x be a vector of events'
covariates, and nw the response network. If you set it up as follows:
nw %v% "b1x" <- c(b1x, rep(0, network.size(nw)-(nw%n%"bipartite")))
nw %v% "b2x" <- c(rep(0, nw%n%"bipartite"), b2x)
then
ergm(nw ~ nodecov("b1x") + nodecov("b2x"))
should fit the model with b1 covariate and b2 covariate, because the
covariate for the b2s in b1x would be all 0s and vice versa. (Of
course, you don't have to put both terms in the model.)
				I hope this helps,
				Pavel

On Wed, 2015-10-14 at 15:32 +0000, Khanna, Aditya [MED] wrote:
Hi Statnet community,

I have been working with some agent-based modelers, and I received a question from them that I didn?t know the answer to. Can one of you please help out? The question pertains to Pavel and colleagues? 2011 paper, Adjusting for network size and composition effect, and is quoted below.


One of the points that the Krivitsky et al. - 2011 paper made was how the network statistics are derived from an egocentric census. E.g., network level properties calculated via f(x_i,x_j) are slightly modified when considering egos and alters (equation 4), whereas actor level statistics are unchanged (equation 5). So this got me thinking about the types of statistics that can be extracted from not just a single level egocentric sample, but what if you ask the alters who THEY talked to etc. (i.e., snowball or forest fire sampling) and if there were any assumptions that Krivitsky?s paper makes that would need  to be adjusted to include those. Specifically, in their discussion section they state:
?We limit our statistics to first- and second-order effects ? dyadic and degree distribution effects ? and do not discuss third-order effects such as triad-closure bias, and while two of the notions of locality that we describe allow modeling of such effects, we do not examine the properties of these in the presence of an offset, because the egocentrically sampled data available do not contain information about such effects.?
This is what prompted my question about any follow up work that they?ve done in this area, as they hinted at wanted to do something in the future (at that time, and maybe in the past now!).

Thanks,
Aditya Khanna
University of Chicago
